hook_text: In 1955, thousands of South Africans were asked one question: if you could make the laws, what would you do?
clip_script: Volunteers knocked on doors across the country with one question. If you could make the laws, what would you do? The answers poured in, on scraps of paper and the backs of leaflets. Give us the vote. Give us land. End the passes. Open the schools. On 25 June 1955, three thousand people gathered on a field at Kliptown. They adopted the Freedom Charter. South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white. The people shall govern. On the second day, armed police surrounded them and took their names. A year later, 156 people were arrested for high treason. The trial dragged on for more than four years. And on 29 March 1961, every remaining accused walked out not guilty.
visual_style: Hands writing demands on scraps of paper; volunteers knocking on doors; black-and-white photos of the crowd at Kliptown; the text of the Freedom Charter scrolling; police with rifles at the edge of the meeting; the accused smiling outside the court; the words 'Not guilty'.
pacing: Gentle start, rising at Kliptown, tense at the arrests, celebratory finish.
